key_terms.meaning: A periodic signal x(t) with period T₀ written as x(t) = Σ over k of cₖ e^{jkω₀t}, a sum of harmonically related sinusoids.
ω₀ = 2π/T₀ rad/s, where T₀ is the smallest period of x(t); every other frequency in the series is an integer multiple kω₀.
x(t) = a₀ + Σ (aₖ cos kω₀t + bₖ sin kω₀t), with a₀ the DC value and aₖ, bₖ the cosine and sine amplitudes.
cₖ = (1/T₀) ∫ over T₀ of x(t) e^{−jkω₀t} dt; c₀ is the average value and |cₖ| is the amplitude of the k-th harmonic.
∫ over T₀ of e^{jmω₀t} e^{−jkω₀t} dt equals T₀ when m = k and 0 otherwise; this is what lets each cₖ be extracted separately.
Sufficient conditions for the series to converge: x(t) is absolutely integrable over one period, has finitely many maxima and minima, and finitely many discontinuities.
Near a jump, the truncated Fourier sum overshoots by about 9 percent of the jump, and the overshoot does not shrink as more terms are added.
X(ω) = ∫ from −∞ to ∞ of x(t) e^{−jωt} dt, a continuous function of ω that describes how much of each frequency an aperiodic signal contains.
x(t) = (1/2π) ∫ from −∞ to ∞ of X(ω) e^{jωt} dω; together with X(ω) it forms a transform pair written x(t) ↔ X(ω).
sinc(x) = sin(πx)/(πx); the rectangular pulse of width τ and height A transforms to Aτ sinc(ωτ/2π).
The range of frequencies over which |X(ω)| is significant; a pulse of shorter duration in time has a wider bandwidth.
If x(t) ↔ X(ω), then x(t − t₀) ↔ X(ω) e^{−jωt₀}; delay changes phase only, not magnitude.
If y(t) = x(t) * h(t), then Y(ω) = X(ω)H(ω); convolution in time becomes multiplication in frequency.
If x(t) ↔ X(ω), then x(t) cos ω_c t ↔ ½[X(ω − ω_c) + X(ω + ω_c)]; multiplying by a carrier shifts the spectrum to ±ω_c.
The energy in the time domain equals the area under |X(ω)|²/2π in frequency; for periodic signals the average power equals Σ |cₖ|².
E_x(ω) = |X(ω)|², in joules per hertz; total energy E = (1/2π) ∫ E_x(ω) dω.
For a periodic or random signal, S(ω) gives the power per hertz; total average power P = (1/2π) ∫ S(ω) dω.
H(ω) = Y(ω)/X(ω) for an LTI system; |H(ω)| scales the amplitude and ∠H(ω) shifts the phase at each frequency.
A channel is distortionless when |H(ω)| = constant and ∠H(ω) = −ωt_d over the signal band, so the output is a scaled, delayed copy of the input.
A magnitude |H(ω)| is realizable by a causal system only if ∫ |ln|H(ω)|| dω is finite, so an exact brick-wall filter is not causal.
R_xx(τ) = ∫ x(t)x(t + τ) dt, measuring how much a signal resembles a shifted copy of itself; R_xx(0) is the energy.
The Fourier transform of the autocorrelation R_xx(τ) is the energy spectral density |X(ω)|².
x̂(t) = (1/π) ∫ x(τ)/(t − τ) dτ, a filter with |H(ω)| = 1 and phase −90° for ω > 0 and +90° for ω < 0.
x_a(t) = x(t) + jx̂(t), whose spectrum is zero for negative frequencies; it gives the envelope and phase of a bandpass signal.

takeaways: Any reasonably well-behaved periodic signal can be built from harmonically related sinusoids, and orthogonality gives a direct formula for each coefficient.
Letting the period T₀ go to infinity turns the discrete harmonic lines of the Fourier series into the continuous spectrum of the Fourier transform.
Properties such as time shift, scaling, convolution and modulation let you get new transform pairs from known ones instead of integrating again.
Parseval's theorem lets you compute energy or power in whichever domain is easier, and tells you where in frequency the energy sits.
An LTI system cannot create new frequencies, so a sinusoid in gives a sinusoid out, changed only in amplitude by |H(ω)| and in phase by ∠H(ω).
Perfect transmission needs a flat magnitude and a linear phase over the signal band; brick-wall filters satisfy this but are not causal, so real designs approximate them.
Correlation and spectral density are a Fourier pair, so similarity-versus-lag in time and energy-versus-frequency carry the same information.
The Hilbert transform is an all-pass 90° phase shifter, and adding j times it to a real signal produces a one-sided spectrum useful in SSB and envelope detection.
bank_note: Long answers here are judged on correct derivation from orthogonality or from the transform definition, a stated property list with the condition for each, and a labelled sketch of the magnitude and phase spectra at the end.

bank.q: Derive the exponential Fourier series of a periodic signal from the orthogonality of complex exponentials, and state how the trigonometric coefficients aₖ, bₖ relate to cₖ.
outline: Write x(t) = Σ cₖ e^{jkω₀t} with ω₀ = 2π/T₀
Multiply by e^{−jnω₀t} and integrate over one period
Use ∫ e^{j(k−n)ω₀t} dt = T₀ when k = n, else 0, so cₙ = (1/T₀)∫ x(t)e^{−jnω₀t}dt
State c₀ = a₀, cₖ = (aₖ − jbₖ)/2 for k > 0, and |cₖ| = ½√(aₖ² + bₖ²)
Note the conjugate symmetry c_{−k} = cₖ* for real x(t)

bank.q: Explain how the Fourier transform is obtained from the Fourier series by letting the period tend to infinity, and interpret the resulting X(ω).
outline: Start from cₖ = (1/T₀)∫ x(t)e^{−jkω₀t}dt over one period
Define T₀cₖ = X(kω₀) and note spacing ω₀ = 2π/T₀ → dω
Let T₀ → ∞ so discrete lines merge into a continuum
x(t) = (1/2π)∫X(ω)e^{jωt}dω follows from the series sum
Interpret |X(ω)| as the density of spectral content, not amplitude of a line

bank.q: State the properties of the Fourier transform: linearity, time shift, frequency shift, time scaling, duality, differentiation, and integration.
outline: Give each property as a transform pair with its formula
Linearity: ax₁ + bx₂ ↔ aX₁ + bX₂
Time shift: x(t − t₀) ↔ X(ω)e^{−jωt₀}
Scaling: x(at) ↔ (1/|a|)X(ω/a)
Duality: X(t) ↔ 2πx(−ω)
Differentiation: dx/dt ↔ jωX(ω)
State one application of each, e.g. shift for delay lines

bank.q: State and prove Parseval's theorem for a periodic signal, and give the energy form for an aperiodic signal.
outline: Periodic: P = (1/T₀)∫|x(t)|²dt = Σ|cₖ|²
Substitute the series and use orthogonality to kill cross terms
Interpret |cₖ|² as the power in the k-th harmonic (two-sided)
Aperiodic: E = ∫|x(t)|²dt = (1/2π)∫|X(ω)|²dω
Define energy spectral density |X(ω)|² in J/Hz

bank.q: Find the exponential Fourier series of a rectangular pulse train of amplitude A, period T₀ and pulse width τ, and sketch the line spectrum.
outline: Write cₖ = (1/T₀)∫ from −τ/2 to τ/2 of A e^{−jkω₀t}dt
Obtain cₖ = (Aτ/T₀) sinc(kτ/T₀)
Show c₀ = Aτ/T₀ is the average value
Note zero crossings at k = T₀/τ and the 1/T₀ line spacing
Sketch two-sided lines with conjugate symmetry and mark the first null

bank.q: Using only the transform of the rectangular pulse and the properties, find the Fourier transforms of (i) a delayed rectangular pulse, (ii) a triangular pulse, (iii) x(t)cos ω_c t for a rectangular x(t).
outline: Start from rect(t/τ) ↔ τ sinc(ωτ/2π)
Delay gives an extra e^{−jωt₀} factor; magnitude unchanged
Triangular pulse is the convolution of two rectangles, so its transform is the square of the sinc, or integrate the property
Modulation theorem halves the pulse spectrum and shifts it to ±ω_c
Sketch spectra to confirm bandwidth doubling

bank.q: An LTI system has h(t) = e^{−at}u(t). Find H(ω), and use it to find the output for input x(t) = cos ω₀t.
outline: H(ω) = 1/(a + jω) from the standard pair e^{−at}u(t) ↔ 1/(a + jω)
|H(ω₀)| = 1/√(a² + ω₀²), ∠H(ω₀) = −tan⁻¹(ω₀/a)
Sinusoid is an eigenfunction: output is |H|cos(ω₀t + ∠H)
Comment that the system is a low-pass with 3 dB point at ω = a
No new frequencies appear at the output

bank.q: For the signal x(t) = A for |t| ≤ τ/2 and zero elsewhere, compute the autocorrelation R_xx(τ_lag) and the energy spectral density, and verify Parseval's theorem.
outline: R_xx(λ) = ∫x(t)x(t+λ)dt is triangular with peak A²τ at λ = 0
Full overlap for |λ| ≤ τ, linear fall to zero at |λ| = τ
Transform gives ESD = A²τ² sinc²(ωτ/2π)
Total energy from time = A²τ; check by integrating the ESD over ω/2π
State Wiener–Khinchin as the link

bank.q: Find the Hilbert transform of (i) cos ω₀t, (ii) a rectangular pulse, and construct the analytic signal of A cos ω₀t.
outline: Hilbert transform of cos ω₀t is sin ω₀t; of sin is −cos
For a rectangular pulse, x̂(t) = (1/π) ln|(t + τ/2)/(t − τ/2)|
Analytic signal A cos ω₀t + jA sin ω₀t = A e^{jω₀t}
Its spectrum has an impulse only at +ω₀
Envelope is A, instantaneous phase is ω₀t

bank.q: Explain why an ideal brick-wall low-pass filter cannot be realised in practice. Support the answer with the impulse response and the Paley–Wiener criterion.
outline: Ideal H(ω) = e^{−jωt_d} for |ω| ≤ ω_c, zero outside
Inverse transform gives h(t) = (ω_c/π) sinc(ω_c(t − t_d)/π), non-zero for t < 0
Non-causal response, and the sinc is not absolutely integrable in the limit
Paley–Wiener: ∫|ln|H||dω must be finite, so |H| cannot be exactly zero over a band
Practical answer: allow a transition band and a tolerance ripple

bank.q: A channel has a non-flat magnitude and a non-linear phase over the signal band. Distinguish amplitude distortion from phase distortion and state the criteria for distortionless transmission.
outline: Distortionless: |H(ω)| = K constant, ∠H(ω) = −ωt_d linear over the band
Amplitude distortion changes relative harmonic amplitudes, altering pulse shape
Phase distortion changes relative delays; group delay d∠H/dω must be constant
Ideal condition cannot hold over all frequencies, so restrict to the band of the signal
Practical criterion: output energy concentrated in the pulse interval, measured by the ratio of in-band to total energy

bank.q: Show that the Hilbert transform is an all-pass filter giving a 90° phase shift, list its main properties, and explain its use in single-sideband modulation.
outline: H(ω) = −j sgn(ω), so |H| = 1 and phase is ∓90°
Two applications give x̂(t) = −x(t), so the inverse is −H
Properties: odd symmetry, energy preserved (Parseval), Hilbert of Hilbert is the negative original
SSB: x_SSB = x(t)cos ω_c t ∓ x̂(t) sin ω_c t cancels one sideband
Analytic signal x + jx̂ has one-sided spectrum

bank.q: Derive the Wiener–Khinchin relation and discuss what it says about the spectral density of white noise and of a periodic signal.
outline: Define R_xx(τ) and write it as a convolution x(τ)*x(−τ)
Take the Fourier transform: FT of x(−τ) is X(−ω) = X*(ω) for real x
Product gives |X(ω)|², the ESD
White noise: flat PSD means a delta autocorrelation, so uncorrelated samples
Periodic signal: PSD is a train of impulses at harmonics with weights |cₖ|²

bank.q: Using the convolution theorem and the frequency response, compare how an LTI system treats a narrow pulse and a long pulse passed through the same low-pass filter.
outline: Narrow pulse has wide spectrum; filter cuts most of it, so severe spreading and energy loss
Long pulse has narrow spectrum inside the passband, so output is nearly undistorted and only delayed
Relationship bandwidth × time duration ≈ constant
Rise time of output set by filter bandwidth, roughly 0.35/B for a first-order response only if stated as approximate
Conclusion: pulse width relative to 1/B decides distortion

glossary.def: A signal that repeats exactly after a fixed interval T₀, so x(t) = x(t + T₀) for all t.
A sinusoid whose frequency is an integer multiple of the fundamental frequency.
The smallest positive value of T₀ for which x(t) = x(t + T₀) holds.
The average value of the signal over one period, given by c₀ or a₀.
A plot of the harmonic amplitudes or phases at discrete frequencies kω₀.
A set of functions whose cross-integral over an interval is zero unless the two functions are the same member.
The property that the partial sums approach the signal at every point of continuity and to the midpoint at a jump.
A signal that does not repeat, so its spectrum is continuous rather than a set of lines.
The description of a signal by the amplitude and phase of each frequency it contains.
Two functions x(t) and X(ω) related by the forward and inverse transform integrals.
The symmetry that lets a known transform pair be reused with the roles of time and frequency exchanged.
The operation y(t) = ∫x(τ)h(t − τ)dτ giving the response of an LTI system to an input.
The output h(t) of an LTI system when the input is a unit impulse δ(t).
The ratio H(ω) = Y(ω)/X(ω), equal to the Fourier transform of the impulse response.
The negative derivative of phase with respect to frequency, −d∠H/dω, giving the delay of a narrow band of frequencies.
Change in pulse shape caused by a phase response that is not linear in frequency.
Change in pulse shape caused by a magnitude response that is not constant over the signal band.
A filter whose magnitude is exactly one in the passband and exactly zero in the stopband, with sharp edges.
A system whose output at any time depends only on present and past inputs, so h(t) = 0 for t < 0.
R_xy(τ) = ∫x(t)y(t + τ)dt, measuring how much one signal resembles a shifted copy of another.
A random signal whose power spectral density is constant at all frequencies.
The slowly varying amplitude |x_a(t)| of a bandpass signal, obtained from the analytic signal.
The Hilbert transform of a signal, in phase quadrature (90° apart) with it.
Another name for the analytic signal x(t) + jx̂(t).
Amplitude modulation in which one sideband is removed, halving the bandwidth, usually with a Hilbert transformer.
